rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ coordinates the clause with an understood “he went”: “then he went and showed him,” as in the omitted “he struck” before the rock split.
rows.anchor: معطوف على محذوف معلوم ، يعني فذهب فأراه

rows.speaker: مقاتل والكلبي
rows.claim: Maqātil and al-Kalbī identify the great sign as Moses’ hand, citing the hand turning white and the sign shown to Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل والكلبي : هي اليد

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ identifies the sign as the staff: the hand only changed color, while the staff became alive, grew, swallowed objects, and then lost its life and form.
rows.anchor: هي العصا ، لأنه ليس في اليد إلا انقلاب لونه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid takes the great sign to be the hand and staff together, since Moses first showed Pharaoh the staff and then the hand.
rows.anchor: وهو أن المراد من الآية الكبرى مجموع اليد والعصا

words: إِنَّ فِى ذَٰلِكَ لَعِبْرَةًۭ لِّمَن يَخْشَىٰٓ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story of Moses and Pharaoh, Pharaoh’s humiliation, and Moses’ triumph warn the God-fearing to abandon rebellion and denial lest they suffer the same punishment.
rows.anchor: فيما اقتصصناه من أمر موسى وفرعون ، وما أحله الله بفرعون من الخزي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers of Muhammad should infer that sharing Pharaoh’s culpable conduct will bring them the same punishment; God supports His prophets and messengers.
rows.anchor: فاعتبروا معاشر المكذبين لمحمد بما ذكرناه ، أي اعلموا أنكم إن شاركتموهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī prefers an argument for resurrection: humans are small beside heaven, so recreating them after death is within God’s power; relative scale matters only in human estimation.
rows.anchor: والمعنى أخلقكم بعد الموت أشد أم خلق السماء أي عندكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative reads the comparison as proof that humans are created; Rāzī calls this weak because deniers of human creation could deny the heaven’s creation too, and the sūra began with resurrection.
rows.anchor: المقصود من هذا الاستدلال بيان كونهم مخلوقين

rows.speaker: الكسائي والفراء والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī, al-Farrāʾ, and al-Zajjāj take the sentence to end at “or the heaven,” making “He built it” a new sentence.
rows.anchor: قال الكسائي والفراء والزجاج : هذا الكلام تم

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم
rows.claim: Abū Ḥātim pauses at “He built it” and connects the phrase to “the heaven,” with an omitted relative pronoun: “the heaven which He built.”
rows.anchor: وعند أبي حاتم الوقف على قوله

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffāl supports the omitted-relative reading with a valid Arabic example; otherwise “He built it” and “raised its height” would be successive unrelated adjectives needing a conjunction.
rows.anchor: قال القفال : يقال : الرجل جاءك عاقل

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ objects that the relative reading implies a heaven that God did not build, which is impossible.
rows.anchor: وللفراء أن يحتج على قوله بأنه لو كان قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī argues that heaven is a body and every body is originated: an eternal body would have to be either moving or at rest.
rows.anchor: الجسم لو كان أزليا لكان في الأزل إما أن يكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eternal motion is impossible because motion means being preceded by another state, whereas eternity excludes any such precedence.
rows.anchor: ماهية الحركة تقتضي المسبوقية بالغير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rest is a positive state, since motion and rest differ only in prior occupancy; heaven moves now, so its rest is removable and contingent, requiring an agent.
rows.anchor: السكون وصف ثبوتي وهو ممكن الزوال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A necessary cause or necessary condition would make rest endure, while a contingent cause leads to regress or a necessary endpoint; a free agent acts by intention, which cannot bring about an already existing state.
rows.anchor: ذلك المؤثر لا بد وأن يكون فاعلا مختارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because a body cannot be eternal either in motion or rest, heaven is originated and needs a maker for its existence and arrangement; reason establishes that its builder is God.
rows.anchor: فثبت بالعقل أن باني السماء هو الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second proof says everything besides the Necessary Existent is possible, originated, and caused: two necessary beings would be composite and dependent, while a caused thing must originate.
rows.anchor: كل ما سوى الواجب فهو ممكن وكل ممكن محدث وكل محدث فعل صانع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third proof says heaven’s size could be a little larger or smaller; its exact measure therefore requires a determiner and builder.
rows.anchor: صريح العقل يشهد بأن جرم السماء لا يمتنع أن يكون أكبر مما هو الآن

rows.speaker: سائل
rows.claim: A proposed objection asks whether God might create a being with power to make bodies, so that this intermediary built heaven.
rows.anchor: خلق شيئا وأعطاه قدرة يتمكن ذلك المخلوق بتلك القدرة

rows.speaker: بعض العلماء
rows.claim: Some scholars say reason proves an originated heaven and an ultimate eternal God, while revelation establishes that God, rather than an intermediary, built it.
rows.anchor: من العلماء من قال : المعلوم بالعقل أنه

rows.speaker: بعض العلماء
rows.claim: Others argue reason excludes an intermediary: all possible things are equally within God’s power, and one effect cannot result from two independent agents.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من قال بل العقل يدل على بطلانه لأنه لما ثبت أن كل ما عداه محدث ثبت أنه قادر لا موجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī calls the second argument sound for those who hold that no effective agent exists besides the One.
rows.anchor: لكن على قول من لا يثبت في الوجود مؤثرا سوى الواحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After stating that God built heaven, the passage turns to explain how He built it.
rows.anchor: واعلم أنه تعالى لما بين في السماء أنه بناها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A thing’s extent measured from top to bottom is its depth, while its extent from bottom to top is its height (samk).
rows.anchor: إذا أخذ من أعلاه إلى أسفله سمي عمقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means that heaven is extremely high; some report that earth and heaven are separated by a journey of five hundred years.
rows.anchor: فالمراد برفع سمكها شدة علوها حتى ذكروا أن ما بين الأرض وبينها مسيرة خمسمائة عام

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others understand the phrase as heaven being raised without pillars, something only God can accomplish.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون : بل المراد : رفع سمكها من غير عمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation takes “He leveled it” to mean that God composed and proportioned heaven.
rows.anchor: وجهان الأول : المراد تسوية تأليفها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the phrase to mean that heaven has no cracks, as in the statement that one sees no disparity in the Merciful’s creation.
rows.anchor: وقيل : بل المراد نفي الشقوق عنها

rows.speaker: القائلون بالقول الأول
rows.claim: Advocates of the first view say the unqualified wording means complete proportion: heaven must be spherical, since other shapes have edges and unequal distances; its sphericity poses no religious harm.
rows.anchor: والقائلون بالقول الأول قالوا

rows.speaker: أصحاب الهيئة
rows.claim: Astronomers have calculated the sizes of celestial bodies and the distances from each to earth.
rows.anchor: بين أصحاب الهيئة مقادير الأجرام الفلكية وأبعاد

rows.speaker: زيد بن عمرو بن نفيل
rows.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl’s poetic line uses daḥāhā for spreading the earth, then describes the mountains being set on it.
rows.anchor: زيد بن عمرو بن نفيل

rows.speaker: أمية بن أبي الصامت
rows.claim: Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt’s verse likewise uses daḥawtu to mean that he spread the lands and leveled them.
rows.anchor: وقال أمية بن أبي الصامت

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: Linguists report two forms, daḥawtu/adḥū and daḥaytu/adḥī, like several paired forms of other verbs.
rows.anchor: قال أهل اللغة في هذه اللفظة

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A report from ʿAlī addresses God as the spreader of the seven earths; al-Rāzī explains the epithet as one who spreads them.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث علي عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One etymology derives daḥw from moving something from place to place: a child tosses a ball across the ground, and an ostrich levels its nest by clearing pebbles.
rows.anchor: أصل الدحو الإزالة للشيء من مكان إلى مكان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent order here puts earth after heaven, while 41:11 says God then turned to heaven, which suggests heaven came after earth.
rows.anchor: ظاهر الآية يقتضي كون الأرض بعد السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reconciliation is that God created earth first as a sphere, created heaven second, then spread the earth; Rāzī notes objections that earth remains spherical and its surface would have to be spread.
rows.anchor: أن الله تعالى خلق الأرض أولا ثم خلق السماء ثانيا ثم دحى الأرض أي بسطها ثالثا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading makes daḥāhā mean preparing earth to produce provisions, an aptitude that comes only after heaven exists, like a father with earth as mother.
rows.anchor: المراد أنه بسطها بسطا مهيأ لنبات الأقوات

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Suddī, and Ibn Jurayj take “after that” as “along with that,” not chronological sequence, as in 68:13 and 90:17.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن جريج أنهم قالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The water is earth’s erupting springs; pasture means grazing, originally the place where grazing occurs.
rows.anchor: ماؤها عيونها المتفجرة بالماء ومرعاها رعيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Earth” and “mountains” are accusative through omitted verbs explained by the later predicates; al-Ḥasan reads both nominative as subjects.
rows.anchor: ونصب الأرض والجبال بإضمار دحا وأرسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The missing conjunction before “brought forth” can be explained by taking spreading as preparation for habitation, then specifying water, pasture, food, and mountains that stabilize the earth.
rows.anchor: معنى دحاها بسطها ومهدها للسكنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “He brought forth” is a circumstantial clause: earth was spread while its water and pasture were brought forth.
rows.anchor: والثاني : أن يكون { أخرج } حالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pasture includes what people and animals eat, as in 16:10’s water and grazing plants and 80:25–32’s account of food and provision.
rows.anchor: أراد بمرعاها ما يأكل الناس والأنعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text metaphorically applies grazing to humans, as with “graze and play”; the reading nartaʿ in 12:12 derives from grazing.
rows.anchor: واستعير الرعي للإنسان كما استعير الرتع

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba takes water and pasture to encompass earth’s provisions and comforts: plants, grains, fruit, wood, clothing, medicine, fire from trees, and salt from water; worldly pleasures stem from water and plants.
rows.anchor: ثم قال ابن قتيبة قال تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī takes the later statement that these are provision for people and livestock as evidence that pasture means everything eaten by both.
rows.anchor: يدل على أنه تعالى أراد بالمرعى كل ما يأكله الناس والأنعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says the explanation of the mountains’ benefits has already been given.
rows.anchor: والكلام في شرح منافع الجبال قد تقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God made these things as enjoyment and benefit for people and their livestock.
rows.anchor: والمعنى أنا إنما خلقنا هذه الأشياء متعة ومنفعة لكم ولأنعامكم

rows.speaker: من قال
rows.claim: Those who argue that God’s acts and rulings are grounded in purposes and benefits cite this verse.
rows.anchor: من قال : إن أفعال الله وأحكامه معللة بالأغراض والمصالح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says the creation of heaven and earth establishes God’s ability to resurrect; after proving resurrection rationally, the passage announces that it will occur.
rows.anchor: ذكر كيفية خلقة السماء والأرض ليستدل بها على كونه قادرا على الحشر والنشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī says Ibn Umm Maktūm (ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shurayḥ ibn Mālik) came while Muḥammad called ʿUtba and Shayba, Abū Jahl, al-ʿAbbās, Umayya, and al-Walīd to Islam; after repeated requests for teaching, the Prophet frowned and turned away, and the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: أتى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ابن أم مكتوم وأم مكتوم أم أبيه واسمه عبدالله بن شريح بن مالك بن ربيعة الفهري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī adds that the Prophet honored Ibn Umm Maktūm, greeting him as the man for whom his Lord reproached him, asking his needs, and appointing him over Medina twice.
rows.anchor: وكان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يكرمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī raises the objection that Ibn Umm Maktūm deserved rebuke: despite blindness he heard the conversation, knew the Prophet’s concern, and interrupted before it ended, harming him.
rows.anchor: ابن أم مكتوم كان يستحق التأديب والزجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection adds that the already Muslim Ibn Umm Maktūm knew his religious needs, while conversion of the unbelieving chiefs might lead many others to Islam; interruption sacrificed a greater good.
rows.anchor: أن الأهم مقدم على المهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection invokes 49:4: if calling the Prophet from behind chambers at the wrong time is censured, an interruption that diverts unbelievers from faith and blocks his chief mission seems worse.
rows.anchor: الذين ينادونك من وراء الحجرات أكثرهم لا يعقلون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection concludes that Ibn’s interruption was sinful and the Prophet’s action was required, then asks why God reproached the Prophet.
rows.anchor: فثبت بهذا أن الذي فعله ابن أم مكتوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second objection says that reproaching the Prophet for merely frowning greatly honors Ibn Umm Maktūm, so calling him “the blind” seems degrading.
rows.anchor: عاتبه على مجرد أنه عبس في وجهه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third objection says the Prophet was authorized to discipline and teach his companions according to what he judged beneficial, so the frown seems to have been permitted.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام كان مأذونا في أن يعامل أصحابه على حسب ما يراه مصلحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One answer is that the outward scene appeared to privilege the rich over the poor and break poor believers’ hearts; Rāzī compares it with 6:52.
rows.anchor: ظاهر الواقعة يوهم تقديم الأغنياء على الفقراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the rebuke may concern an inward inclination toward the nobles for kinship and rank and aversion to the blind man for his lack of kinship and status, not the outward act itself.
rows.anchor: لعل هذا العتاب لم يقع على ما صدر من الرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling him blind is not belittling: his blindness is precisely why he deserved greater kindness and compassion.
rows.anchor: ذكره بلفظ الأعمى ليس لتحقير شأنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though the Prophet could discipline his companions, this incident seemed to place the wealthy before the poor and worldly concerns before religion, so it prompted the rebuke.
rows.anchor: كان مأذونا في تأديب أصحابه لكن ههنا لما أوهم
